title: 5. Verification
text: Agents produce plausible code. Verification is the part of the workflow that is yours, and it is short enough to do every single time.

title: 5. Verification
text:
The four-step minimum

Read the diff. git diff before you commit, or the diff in the pull request. If you cannot explain a change, do not merge it.
Check the coding against the codebook. Open the PDF. Confirm the response options, the missing-data codes, and the direction of the scale.
Report n_obs and n_miss. Every model, every time. If the N moved and nobody said why, cases were silently dropped.
Write the test. A check you run once is a check you will stop running.

title: 5. Verification
text:
Reporting N
voters <- wss |> filter(!is.na(trump_vote))
cat("n_obs =", nrow(voters),
    "| n_miss =", nrow(wss) - nrow(voters), "\n")

fit <- glm(trump_vote ~ latino * year, family = quasibinomial,
           weights = weight, data = voters)
cat("n_obs =", nobs(fit), "| n_miss =", nrow(voters) - nobs(fit), "\n")
The second pair matters most: listwise deletion inside a model formula is the most common way a sample shrinks without anyone noticing.

title: 5. Verification
section: Turning a check into a test

title: 5. Verification
text:
Checking an agent’s factual claims







Claim it makes
How you check it




“pid7 runs 1–7 with 4 as independent”
The codebook, not the data’s range


“I dropped non-voters”
n_miss, and count() on the raw variable


“This uses survey weights”
Read the call. Look for weights =


“The 2024 weight is weight”
It is weight_all. See AGENTS.md


“Smith (2019) shows…”
Search for the citation. Assume it is invented




Reproducibility is the real test Delete data/wss_clean.rds and output/, then run the pipeline from the top. If the numbers come back identical, the work is reproducible. If they do not, something lives in a console somewhere instead of in a script.

title: 5. Verification
text:
What to trust

Trust code you have read and can explain.
Trust numbers that a script regenerates from raw data.
Do not trust a result that exists only in a chat transcript.
Do not trust your own memory of what you accepted ten minutes ago. That is what the commit history is for.

title: 1. Setup
text:
GitHub hosts code, data, and documents on the web. Four reasons it matters for research:

Transparency — the work is open to inspection.
Reproducibility — others can recreate and extend your analysis.
Collaboration — several people contribute to one project without emailing files.
Version control — every change is tracked, and reverting is trivial.


And for working with agents An agent edits files in place. The repository is what makes that safe: you can see exactly what changed (git diff) and undo it (git restore). Without version control, you are letting a confident stranger type into your manuscript.

What a repository looks like
A repository is a folder with your code, data, documentation, and the complete history of changes. This one:
UNM_Workshop/
├── AGENTS.md              the brief every AI agent reads
├── CLAUDE.md              one line: @AGENTS.md
├── data/
│   ├── wss_2020_2024.csv  analysis file (read-only)
│   └── wss_clean.rds      built by R/01_recode.R
├── codebooks/             2020 & 2024 survey codebooks (PDF)

│   ├── 00_build_data.R    raw Stata → csv (instructor only)

text:
AI as a Research Tool


A hands-on workshop


University of New Mexico · Albuquerque · Christopher Weber, University of Arizona

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
Goals

Everyone can clone, branch, and open a pull request on a shared project.
Everyone has an agent that knows this project through an instruction file.
We answer one substantive question together — and check the machine’s work.


Before you arrive A GitHub account, and your username sent to me so I can add you as a collaborator. Everything else can be done in the browser through Module 1.

title: 0. Framing: what is “AI” here?
text:
A large language model predicts text. A coding agent wraps that model in a loop: it reads files, proposes edits, runs commands, reads the output, and tries again. Three consequences follow, and they explain everything else on this site.

It has no memory of your project beyond what it reads this session. That is why an instruction file (Module 3) matters more than clever prompting.
It optimizes for a plausible answer, not a correct one. It will invent a variable name, a function argument, or a citation with complete fluency.
It acts on your files. Which is fine — if every change is visible and reversible (Module 2).

title: 0. Framing: what is “AI” here?
text:
Software engineering vs. research code
Agents arrived from software engineering, where they are genuinely strong. Research code is a different problem.









Software
Research code




Where the spec lives
Written down; tests encode it
A codebook, a literature, your judgment


How failure appears
Loud — it crashes or a test goes red
Silent — it runs and prints a number


Cost of a subtle error
A bug report
A published claim


Agent performance
Strong
Confidently wrong




The core asymmetry A wrong recode does not throw an error. pid7 == 8 is “not sure” in this survey, not “strong Republican” — code it as the latter and your partisanship measure is quietly wrong, every model after it is wrong, and nothing in your console will say so.

title: 0. Framing: what is “AI” here?
section: What to delegate, and what never to trust unchecked
text:
What to delegate, and what never to trust unchecked

Delegate freely Scaffolding and boilerplate · refactoring you can read · documentation · tests · debugging an error message · “explain what this script does” · translating Stata to R · the fiddly ggplot2 call you do not want to look up.


Never accept unchecked Variable coding and reverse-coding · which cases were dropped · weights and survey design · anything that cites a number · anything that cites a source.

title: 0. Framing: what is “AI” here?
text:
Where the tools differ

Copilot is strongest at the next line: inline completion while you type, and quick questions about an open file.
Claude Code (and Codex, Cursor’s agent mode, Copilot agent mode) is strongest at the next task: “add income terciles to the recode, rerun it, and show me what changed.” It edits several files and runs commands.
A chat window with no repository access is the weakest option for this work: it cannot see your data, so it guesses your variable names.

Use the first two together. That is what we set up next.

Discussion Name one task in your own current project you would hand to an agent today, and one you would not. What distinguishes them?

title: 3. Agents: instructions & shortcuts
text:
What ours says
## Project
Did Latino voters in the Western states shift toward Trump from 2020
to 2024, and does authoritarianism condition that shift?

## Layout
- data/wss_2020_2024.csv  analysis file (read-only; never edit by hand)
- R/01_recode.R           all recoding lives here
- codebooks/              cite these when describing a variable

## Rules
- R + tidyverse, native pipe |>. Minimal comments.
- New recodes go in R/01_recode.R, not in analysis scripts.
- Always report n_obs and n_miss with any model.
- Use survey weights for population estimates; say when you don't.
- Don't push to main without the user's say-so; prefer a branch + PR.

title: 3. Agents: instructions & shortcuts
text:
Writing a good AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md

What the project is (one sentence) and the research question.
Where things live; which files are read-only.
Variable definitions and where to cite them (codebook).
Conventions: language, style, where recodes go.
Guardrails: report N and missingness, use weights, don’t push to main.
Keep it short; agents follow concise rules better than essays.

Bootstrap one: run /init in Claude Code, then edit it yourself. Personal, all-project preferences go in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.

title: 3. Agents: instructions & shortcuts
text:
Division of labor
Copilot is strongest at the next line — completions while you type. Claude Code is strongest at the next task — “add income terciles to the recode, rerun it, and show me what changed.” Use both.

title: 3. Agents: instructions & shortcuts
text:
Spending less

/clear between unrelated tasks; long context is re-billed every turn.
Point at files (@R/02_analysis.R) rather than asking it to “look around.”
Plan mode for anything large: approve the plan, then let it execute.
A smaller model for routine edits and renames.
One well-specified request beats six vague corrections.


Then verify Agents produce plausible code, and in research code failure is silent. Read the diff, check the coding against the codebook, report n_obs and n_miss, and write a test. That is Module 5.

title: 2. Git workflow
text:
Working directory → Staging area → Local repo → Remote (GitHub)
     (edit)            (add)        (commit)        (push)
                                         ←  (pull)  ←
Changes move left to right, one deliberate step at a time, and come back with git pull. The staging area exists so you can commit some of your changes — the finished recode, not the half-written one beside it.

title: 2. Git workflow
text:
Fork vs. clone
Fork makes a copy of someone else’s repository under your account, on the GitHub website. Use it when you want to contribute to a project you cannot write to. Fork + clone + pull request is how open-source collaboration works.
Clone makes a copy on your computer:
git clone https://github.com/crweber9874/UNM_Workshop.git
cd UNM_Workshop
Your edits stay local until you push, and you can only push to repositories you have access to.

Today Everyone is a collaborator on one repository, so you clone and work on branches. If you would rather keep your work separate, fork first and open pull requests from your fork — the workflow below is otherwise identical.

title: 2. Git workflow
text:
The everyday loop
git pull                     # ALWAYS first: get everyone else's work
git status                   # what changed?
git add R/01_recode.R        # stage specific files (avoid `git add .` blindly)
git commit -m "Recode age into generations"
git push
A commit is a snapshot of your changes with a unique ID and a message. The message is for the version of you who, in four months, needs to know why age_group has four categories. Write it for that person.

title: 2. Git workflow
text:
Working together in one repository
git pull
git switch -c weber-recode-generation     # your own branch
# ...edit, add, commit...
git push -u origin weber-recode-generation
gh pr create --fill                       # open a pull request
Someone reviews the pull request on GitHub and merges it. Then everyone returns to a common base:
git switch main && git pull

text:
When to use what








Action
When
Command




Fork

on github.com

Getting a repo onto your machine

Choosing what goes in the commit

Push
Publishing your branch

Pull request
Asking for review and a merge

Rules of the road Pull before you start, push when you stop · one person per file where possible (recode / analysis / app) · small commits with clear messages · never commit data you were not given, passwords, or .Renviron.

text:
Merge conflicts
<<<<<<< HEAD
your version
=======
their version
>>>>>>> main
Keep what is right, delete the markers, then git add and git commit. You can ask the agent — “resolve the merge conflict in R/01_recode.R, keeping both recodes” — and then read its diff.

Undo



Situation
Command




See what you changed
git diff


Discard edits to a file
git restore file.R


Unstage
git restore --staged file.R


Fix the last commit message
git commit --amend (before pushing)


Undo a pushed commit
git revert <hash>


Look at the history
git log --oneline -10




Your turn Create a branch, add tmp/<lastname>.qmd with a sentence about your own data, commit it, push it, and open a pull request. Then review someone else’s.

title: 4. The pipeline & the group project
text:
Did Latino voters in the Western states shift toward Trump between 2020 and 2024, and does authoritarianism condition that shift?
Western States Survey (YouGov), 2020 (n = 3,600) and 2024 (n = 4,000): Arizona, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah. Codebooks: 2020, 2024.

latino — the YouGov race item (Hispanic).
authoritarianism — mean of four child-rearing pairs, 0–1, 1 = authoritarian response (auth1–auth4).
trump_vote — 1 Trump, 0 Biden/Harris, NA otherwise.
Weights — weight in 2020, weight_all in 2024, combined as weight.


Cite the codebook, not the agent Every claim about a variable on this page traces to codebooks/ and the variable list in AGENTS.md. When an agent tells you what a variable means, that is a hypothesis.

title: 4. The pipeline & the group project
text:
Run it end to end
Rscript R/01_recode.R                       # csv  -> data/wss_clean.rds
Rscript R/02_analysis.R                     # models, figures -> output/
Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")'

Why the order is enforced Every number traces back through exactly one path. If the recode changes, the analysis and the app change with it, because neither keeps its own private copy of the recoding logic. Ask an agent to add a recode to 02_analysis.R and it will happily do it — this is the rule you are enforcing against your own convenience.

title: 4. The pipeline & the group project
text:
Where we start
Weighted two-party Trump share:




2020
2024
Change




Non-Latino
.503 (n = 1,944)
.511 (n = 2,828)
+.008


Latino
.398 (n = 937)
.419 (n = 786)
+.021



n_obs = 6,495 two-party voters · n_miss = 1,105 (non-voters, other candidates, ineligible) of 7,600 respondents.

The puzzle A two-point Latino shift, estimated on 786 Latino respondents in 2024, is far from the double-digit national exit-poll story. Sample? Weights? Mode? Reported versus intended vote? That is the group task — not to reproduce a headline, but to establish what this sample can and cannot support.

Source: R/02_analysis.R run on data/wss_clean.rds. The intervals in that script use a Kish effective n, not a design-based variance — fixing that is a legitimate first contribution.

title: 4. The pipeline & the group project
text:
Four teams

Recode team — add generation, income terciles, and a strength-of-partisanship measure to R/01_recode.R. Check each against the codebook, and add a test per variable.
Analysis team — Bayesian logit with brms; predicted probabilities for authoritarianism × Latino × year. Does the reported/intended distinction (vote_type) matter?
Shiny team — add a state-by-year panel and a download button to app/app.R.
Skeptics — is this sample representative of Latino voters? Interrogate the weights, the mode, and the comparison with external estimates.


Workflow for every team Branch → work with your agent → read the diff → report n_obs and n_miss → commit → pull request. Review someone else’s PR before you ask for yours.

title: 4. The pipeline & the group project
text:
Starting prompts worth stealing
Read AGENTS.md and R/01_recode.R. Add an income-tercile variable built from
faminc, using survey weights. Do not touch anything else. Show me the diff.

Read codebooks/wss2024_codebook.pdf for pid7 and tell me whether
R/01_recode.R codes party3 correctly. Quote the codebook.

Refit the model in R/02_analysis.R with brms, bernoulli family, weakly
informative priors. Report n_obs and n_miss. Do not drop the weights.
Each of these is narrow, names its files, and asks for evidence. That is the whole technique.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
The Premise


A coding agent is a collaborator with no memory and no stake in being right. It writes plausible code quickly, and plausible is not the same as correct.
The useful question is not can it write the model? It is what work can I delegate, and how do I check it?
Three things make delegation safe: a repository (so every change is visible and reversible), an instruction file (so the agent knows the project), and a habit of verification (so you catch what it got wrong).
Everything today runs on one shared repo and one real research question.



Three goals

Everyone can clone, branch, and open a pull request on a shared project.
Everyone has an agent that knows this project through an instructions file.
We answer one substantive question together — and check the machine’s work.

1 · Setup GitHub, Copilot, Claude Code, Codespaces
2 · Git Pull, branch, commit, push, pull request

Slides, instructions, and data: https://crweber9874.github.io/UNM_Workshop/ · Repository: https://github.com/crweber9874/UNM_Workshop

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
Software Engineering vs. Research Code



SOFTWARE
Tests tell you it works. The spec is written down. Correctness is checkable by the machine.

Agents are strong here
Failures are loud






RESEARCH
The spec lives in a codebook and your judgment. A wrong recode runs fine and produces a publishable number.

Agents are confidently wrong here
Failures are silent




This asymmetry drives every rule we adopt today. The agent can scaffold, refactor, document, and debug. It cannot know that pid7 == 8 is “not sure” rather than “strong Republican” unless the codebook says so and you make it read it.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
Why a Repository at All

GitHub hosts code, data, and documents on the web. Four reasons it matters for research:

Transparency — the work is open to inspection.
Reproducibility — others can recreate and extend your analysis.
Collaboration — several people contribute to one project without emailing files.
Version control — every change is tracked, and reverting is trivial.



And for working with agents
An agent edits files in place. The repository is what makes that safe: you can see exactly what it changed (git diff), and undo it (git restore). Without version control, you are letting a confident stranger type into your dissertation.

Housekeeping The free tier is 60 core-hours a month. Stop your codespace when you are done — it bills while it idles.


Your turn 1. Open the repository and start a codespace (or clone locally). 2. In the terminal: gh auth status — are you signed in? 3. Start claude, then type /init and read what it writes about this project.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
Fork vs. Clone



FORK
A copy of someone else’s repository under your account, made on the GitHub website.

Use it to contribute where you lack write access
Fork + clone + pull request = open-source collaboration






CLONE
A copy of a repository on your computer, made with git clone <url>.

Your edits stay local until you push
You can only push to repos you have access to




Today everyone is a collaborator on one repo, so you clone and work on branches. Send me your GitHub username if you are not added yet; fork instead if you would rather keep your work separate.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
Get the Repository
git clone https://github.com/crweber9874/UNM_Workshop.git
cd UNM_Workshop

From RStudio you can do all of this in Tools → Terminal → New Terminal, or point-and-click in the Git tab. The commands are the same underneath, and the terminal is what you will be able to explain to a collaborator — or to an agent.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
The Everyday Loop
git pull                        # ALWAYS first: get everyone else's work
git status                      # what did I change?
git add R/01_recode.R           # stage specific files, not `git add .` blindly
git commit -m "Add generation recode"
git push

What a commit is
A snapshot of your changes with a unique ID and a message. The message is for the version of you who, in four months, needs to know why age_group has four categories. Write it for that person.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
Working Together Without Collisions
git pull
git switch -c weber-recode-generation    # your own branch
# ...edit, add, commit...
git push -u origin weber-recode-generation
gh pr create --fill                      # open a pull request

Someone reviews the pull request on GitHub and merges it. Then everyone returns to a common base: git switch main && git pull.


Rules of the road Pull before you start, push when you stop · one person per file where possible (recode / analysis / app) · small commits with clear messages · never commit data you were not given, passwords, or .Renviron.

title: AI as a Research Tool
section: How an Agent Sees This Repository
text:
How an Agent Sees This Repository


On start it loads instruction files: CLAUDE.md (Claude Code), AGENTS.md (Copilot, Codex, Cursor, and others), .github/copilot-instructions.md (Copilot).
It reads what you point at — @R/01_recode.R — or what it finds by searching.
It runs commands — R, git, shell — with your permission.



So the instruction file is the project brief
Layout, variable meanings, conventions, guardrails. Here CLAUDE.md contains one line, @AGENTS.md, so every tool in the room shares a single source of truth. Change the brief once and all of them follow it.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
Anatomy of a Good AGENTS.md

## Project
Did Latino voters in the Western states shift toward Trump from 2020
to 2024, and does authoritarianism condition that shift?

## Layout
- data/wss_2020_2024.csv  analysis file (read-only; never edit by hand)
- R/01_recode.R           all recoding lives here
- codebooks/              cite these when describing a variable

## Rules
- R + tidyverse, native pipe |>. Minimal comments.
- New recodes go in R/01_recode.R, not in analysis scripts.
- Always report n_obs and n_miss with any model.
- Use survey weights for population estimates; say when you don't.
- Don't push to main without the user's say-so; prefer a branch + PR.


What the project is · where things live · which files are read-only · variable definitions and where to cite them · conventions · guardrails. Keep it short: agents follow concise rules far better than essays. Bootstrap one with /init, then edit it yourself — the draft will be describing your code, not your intentions.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
Verify, Always



DELEGATE

Scaffolding and boilerplate
Refactoring you can read
Documentation and tests
Debugging an error message
“Explain what this script does”






NEVER TRUST UNCHECKED

Variable coding and reverse-coding
Which cases got dropped
Weights and survey design
Anything citing a number
Anything citing a source




The minimum check, every time: read the diff, confirm the coding against the codebook, and look at n_obs and n_miss. If the N moved and nobody said why, something was silently dropped.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
The Question

Did Latino voters in the Western states shift toward Trump between 2020 and 2024, and does authoritarianism condition that shift?
Western States Survey (YouGov), 2020 and 2024: Arizona, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah. Latino is the YouGov race item; authoritarianism is the mean of four child-rearing pairs, scored 0–1 with 1 the authoritarian response.


Variable definitions and coding: codebooks/wss2020_codebook.pdf, codebooks/wss2024_codebook.pdf, and the variable list in AGENTS.md. Cite the codebook, not the agent.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
Run It End to End
Rscript R/01_recode.R                       # csv  -> data/wss_clean.rds
Rscript R/02_analysis.R                     # models, figures -> output/
Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")'
Rscript -e 'shiny::runApp("app")'

Why this order is enforced
Every number in the paper traces back through exactly one path. If the recode changes, the analysis and the app change with it, because neither one keeps its own private copy of the recoding logic. Ask the agent to add a recode to 02_analysis.R and it will happily do it — this is the rule you are enforcing against your own convenience.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
Where We Start




Weighted two-party Trump share
2020
2024
Change




Non-Latino
.503 (n = 1,944)
.511 (n = 2,828)
+.008


Latino
.398 (n = 937)
.419 (n = 786)

n_obs = 6,495 two-party voters · n_miss = 1,105 (non-voters, other candidates, ineligible) of 7,600 respondents.


The puzzle A two-point Latino shift, on 786 Latino respondents in 2024, is far from the double-digit national exit-poll story. Sample? Weights? Mode? Reported versus intended vote? That is the group task — not to reproduce a headline, but to work out what this sample can and cannot support.


Produced by R/02_analysis.R from data/wss_clean.rds; weights are weight (2020) and weight_all (2024). Confidence intervals in the script use a Kish effective n, not a design-based variance.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
Four Teams


Recode Generations, income terciles, strength of partisanship — each checked against the codebook
Analysis brms logit; predicted probabilities for authoritarianism × Latino × year. Does vote_type (reported vs. intended) matter?
Shiny A state-by-year panel and a download button
Skeptics Is this sample representative of Latino voters? Weighting, mode, and comparison with external estimates



Workflow for every team Branch → work with your agent → read the diff → report n_obs and n_miss → commit → pull request. Review someone else’s PR before you ask for yours.

title: AI as a Research Tool
AI as a Research Tool
text:
Wrap-up


What to take home



The repository is the safety net. Branch, diff, revert — then an agent editing your files is a convenience rather than a risk.
The instruction file is the real interface. One brief, every tool, short enough to be followed.
Agents are strong where failure is loud and weak where it is silent. Research code is mostly the second kind.
Verification is not optional and not vague: read the diff, cite the codebook, report n_obs and n_miss, write the test.
One pipeline, one path from raw data to the published number.



Today’s deliverable: a merged pull request from every team, and a number each of us can defend.
